newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH BONDS END LOWER ON GREENSPAN COMMENTS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH BONDS END LOWER ON GREENSPAN COMMENTS.

text.p: 1655 GMT - Dutch bonds dive on Greenspan's hawkish testimony
but rebound in line with Bunds as Germany decouples from U.S.
Fed chief's comments enliven think trading. Short end pressured
in early trading, leading to curve flattening.
* Feb 2007s 102.03/11 (-0.37), bid yield 5.48 pct (highest
more than two weeks), steady -11 bp to Jan 2007 Bunds.
Jan 2024 Bunds versus -22 bp pvs close.
* Spreads: 10/2 yr 203 bp vs 208, 10/5 yr 90 bp vs 90.
"When Greenspan spoke, the market came off. It's trying to find new levels," said one dealer.
He expected Dutch bonds to bounce off current levels, reasoning they were oversold before Greenspan's statements hit traders' screens.
The yield on the 10-year benchmark, the February 2006 Dutch state loan, ended at 5.48 percent, its highest level in more than two weeks, compared with 5.43 percent on Tuesday.
One trader noted that after initial underperformance in the morning, German and Dutch paper outperformed the longer end of their respective curves in the sell-off.
Dutch 1999 and 2000 paper was mentioned as having been under pressure in morning trading. "In the morning there was a lot of selling in the front-end," the trader said.
This contributed to a slight flattening of the guilder yield curve, with the spread between 10 and two year yields narrowing to 203 basis points from 208.
One broker said the few buyers prepared to make bids found ready sellers. "The few we did (have) got hit," she said, adding that trading volumes were low.
Another dealer said the German and Dutch markets did not react as adversely as U.S. Treasuries to Greenspan.
He said this represented a "sort of decoupling" of the German and U.S. bond markets.
"This news is basically nothing to do with Germany," he said.
He also noted an emptiness in the Dutch market, attributing this to speculation of a hike in the special advances rate, which sets the tone for Dutch money rates.
Such a rise would produce a less favourable "carry" for investors, he said.
-- Garry West, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
